8.2.1 SOME TERMS USED IN BIOLOGY 1. Level of organization: Depending upon the number and degree of complexity or specialization of cells present in an animal, following body organizations are found in animals: i. Cellular level of body organization: In primitive multicellular organisms like sponges, there is no co-ordination among the cells and cells are not organized to form tissues. Individual cell performs its own function. This is cellular level of body organization. ii. Tissue level of body organization: In coeleneterates, certain cells are organized together to form tissues which is called tissue level of body organization. Example: Nerve cells forming nerve net in Hydra. iii. Organ-system level of body organization: In multicellular animals from platyhelminthes to chordates, tissues are aggregated into organs and organs are coordinated or associated to form a particular system performing specific function such as digestion, circulation, respiration etc. 2. Body plan: body plan in animals can be divided into following types: i. Cell aggregate plan: In this, body consists of aggregation of many cells where individual cell functions independently. There is no tissue formation in this type of body plan. It is only found in porifera phylum.
Figure 8.2.1 Cell aggregate body plan in sponges ii. Blind sac plan: Body contains a single cavity which blindly ends at the posterior side.
There is a single opening at the anterior end. It is found in coelenterates and some platyhelminthes.

Figure 8.2.2 Blind sac body plan in Hydra iii. Tube within tube plan: This type body plan consists of two tubes, one of which is formed by body wall and within it lies another tube of digestive tract. Digestive tract is a complete tube with openings at both ends. Animals from nemathelminthes phylum up to chordata have this type of body plan. It is of following types:

Figure 8.2.3 Tube within tube body plan in fish a. Protostomic plan: In the embryo, Mouth develops before the anus. Example: roundworms, annelids, arthropods, molluscs and such animals are called protostomes. b. Deuterostomic plan: Anus develops before the mouth in embryo. Example: echinoderms and chordates and these animals are called deuterostomes. 3. Body symmetry i. Asymmetrical body: When the body of an animal cannot be divided into two similar halves through any plane, it is called an asymmetrical body. Example: Amoeba, most of the sponges etc.

ii. Symmetrical body: An animal’s body is said to be symmetrical if it can be divided into two similar halves through one or more planes. It is of following types: a. Spherical symmetry: In this type of symmetry, body shape is spherical and body can be divided into two similar halves in any plane that runs through the centre of organism. Example: Volvox, Streptococcus

b. Radial symmetry: In this, body can be divided into roughly two equal halves by any
one of many vertical planes passing through the central axis. Generally, these
animals are cylinder like in form and similar parts of the body are arranged equally
around the axis. Example: most of the coelenterates and adult echinoderms.

Figure 8.2.6 Radially symmetrical animals c. Bilateral symmetry: In this type of symmetry, only one median vertical plane divides the whole body into two equal halves. From the phylum Platyhelminthes to Chordata, all animals show bilateral symmetry with few exceptions in molluscs and echinoderms.
Figure 8.2.7 Bilaterally symmetrical animals Biology, Grade 11 | 317
d. Biradial symmetry: In this type of symmetry, Animals body show a combination of both bilateral and radial symmetry. Example: comb jellies.
